conventions.ranges: [low, high]; a single sourced value is given as [v, v]
conventions.derived: Values marked derived:true are simple arithmetic on the cited source figures (method in note); nothing is estimated beyond the sources
conventions.nulls: null means no acceptable source was found in this pass; see the note
conventions.oldFlag: oldData:true when the underlying figure is from before 2016 (or undated); prices flagged oldPrice:true when the price year is before 2020

laying_hens.minGroupSizeNote: Chickens are flock animals, but no cited extension minimum was found; do not quote a number.
laying_hens.starterFlockNote: University of Maryland backyard budget uses 10 hens. Penn State suggests 50 to 100 hens for a beginning egg business.
laying_hens.spaceIndoorNote: 1.5 sq ft is the minimum in Penn State's commercial small-scale guide. Backyard guidance is 3 to 4 (extension.org) or 3 to 5 (UMN).
laying_hens.spaceOutdoorNote: extension.org backyard guideline. The source notes that little peer-reviewed research exists on backyard space.
laying_hens.feedNote: UMN: a 6-lb hen eats about 3 lb a week (about 156 lb a year). Penn State organic budget: 90 lb per bird over 52 production weeks. UMD: 4.5 lb of feed per dozen eggs.
laying_hens.waterNote: No extension per-hen figure found (the NDSU water table omits poultry). Provide continuous access.

production.eggsNote: UMN: about 6 eggs a week at peak (about 312 a year). Low end derived from UMD's 70% average hen-day rate x 365 = 255.
production.ageDecline: UF/IFAS: production peaks at about 90% 6-8 weeks after lay begins (18-22 weeks of age) and falls to about 65% after 12 months of lay. Many hens decline significantly after 2-3 years. Molt comes after 50-60 weeks of lay. UMN: laying starts around 6 months, is highest in the first two years, and hens live 5-10 years.
production.lightNote: UF: about 14 h. Penn State: never exceed 16 h.

laying_hens.laborNote: UMD: 20 min a day for 10 hens (2.3 h/wk) and 0.5 h a day for 100 hens (3.5 h/wk). Penn State egg business: 180-200 h a year.
laying_hens.startupNote: UMD 10-hen budget: housing $500, heater $50, feeder and waterer $75, storage $50, 10 chicks at $6 = $735. UMD 100-hen budget: $1,950 for housing and equipment only. HomeGuide (2024-26): small DIY coop $250-500, prefab $800-4,000+.
laying_hens.annualNote: UMD 10-hen flock, 3-year average of $1,759 total (feed at $15 per 50 lb). Cost per dozen: $3.37 for 10 hens and $2.07 for 100 hens, excluding labor.
laying_hens.priceYearNote: UMD fact sheet FS-2025-0783 (2025). The UMD 100-hen budget page is undated.
regulatory: No rooster is needed for eggs (UMN does not list one as necessary). Roosters and flock size are often limited by municipal zoning; check local code.

Penn State egg sales guidance: keep eggs at 45°F or below within 24 h of lay. It cites a threshold for flocks under 3,000 laying hens that sell within 5 days of lay. State egg-handler licensing varies.
laying_hens.climate: UF: heat depresses feed intake, egg production and egg size. Supplemental light is needed in short days.
laying_hens.predators: UMN: raccoons, rats, owls, hawks, cats.
laying_hens.welfare: Nest boxes: one per 4-5 hens (UMN). Continuous fresh water, layer feed with at least 16% protein and 3.5% calcium (Penn State).

Small-Scale Egg Production (Organic and Conventional), Penn State

meat_chickens.unit: per bird (Cornish cross broiler), per grow-out
meat_chickens.starterFlockNote: The Missouri small-scale budget runs 100 birds per batch and 7 batches a year. A household may raise far fewer. No household-size source was found.
meat_chickens.spaceIndoorNote: Penn State pasture: 1.5 sq ft per bird (a 10x12 ft Salatin tractor holds 80 birds). extension.org confinement: 3-4 sq ft.
meat_chickens.spaceOutdoorNote: extension.org: outdoor access is not necessary for commercial strains, which are less likely to use it.
meat_chickens.feedNote: Penn State: about 15 lb per bird to harvest weight. Missouri G742 budget implies about 7.3 lb per bird. These conflict; prefer the Penn State figure for planning.
meat_chickens.growOutNote: Penn State: 6-8 weeks. Slow-growing breeds take 8-9 weeks.
meat_chickens.waterNote: Penn State: about 3.6 gal per bird over the whole grow-out, not per day.

production.note: Penn State: 5.25 lb live gives a 4 lb carcass (75% dressing) at about 6 weeks. Missouri: 6.5 lb live at 70% gives 4.55 lb.

meat_chickens.laborNote: Missouri G742: 8.8 h/wk and 220.5 h a year for 100-bird batches, 7 batches a year.
meat_chickens.startupNote: Missouri G742 small-scale mobile pen system, including on-farm processing equipment.
meat_chickens.costPerBirdNote: Missouri G742 small-scale variable cost per bird, including on-farm processing at $4.27 per bird.
meat_chickens.priceYearNote: The G742 page gives no year.
regulatory: USDA PPIA exemptions: Producer/Grower 1,000-bird limit and 20,000-bird limit (including PGPR and small enterprise). Birds must be healthy and processed under sanitary conditions. Containers must carry the producer name, address and 'Exempt P.L. 90-492'. No interstate sales. Only one exemption per operation. States may be stricter (ACES 2022).
meat_chickens.climate: Fast-growing broilers are heat-sensitive. No numeric threshold was sourced.
meat_chickens.predators: Pasture pens and tractors protect against predators. No specific source.
meat_chickens.welfare: Cornish cross grow very fast. Penn State notes slow-growing alternatives (Freedom Ranger and others, 8-9 wk, 67-69% dressing).

sources.title: A Quick Guide to Raising Pastured Broilers (Penn State)
Mobile Poultry for Meat Planning Budget G742 (MU Extension)
Space allowances for small and backyard poultry (extension.org)
Exemptions from USDA Inspection for Small-Scale Poultry Processors (Alabama Extension)

ducks_layers.spaceOutdoorNote: extension.org gives no outdoor recommendation for ducks.
ducks_layers.feedNote: extension.org: laying ducks eat about 120 g (0.25 lb) a day; x 365 = about 91 lb. Ducklings eat about 27.6 lb to 20 weeks. Ducks use 20-30% more feed per dozen eggs than chickens.

production.eggsNote: extension.org: commercial laying ducks 300-350. Oklahoma State breeds site: some Khaki Campbell strains average about 300. Duck eggs weigh 32-34 oz a dozen.

regulatory: Zoning for poultry usually applies to ducks too; check local code. Egg-sale rules are the same as for chickens (state egg law).
ducks_layers.climate: Oklahoma State: Khaki Campbells lay well without artificial light.

sources.title: Feeding ducks for egg production in small flocks (extension.org)
Khaki Campbell Ducks (Oklahoma State University Breeds of Livestock)
Space allowances for small and backyard poultry (extension.org)

meat_rabbits.starterFlockNote: UMaine and Texas A&M: 4-5 breeding does and 1 buck for family production.
meat_rabbits.spaceIndoorNote: Doe cage 30x30x18 in (6.25 sq ft). Buck cage 30x24 or 24x24 in. Nest box 10x16x8 in.
meat_rabbits.feedNote: UMaine budget: about 175 lb per doe per year, including her litters to fryer weight as budgeted. Free-choice feeding.

production.note: Dressing percent was not found in the fetched extension sources.

meat_rabbits.laborNote: UMaine: about 20 h per breeding doe per year. 4 does = 80 h a year, about 15 min a day. Weekly figure derived (80/52).
meat_rabbits.annualNote: UMaine: annual operating cost per doe $195, return over costs $67.50 per doe (Jan 2014 prices). Texas A&M: feed $74 per doe (1995 prices).
regulatory: Texas A&M (1995) says Texas did not require inspection of rabbit processing. Rabbit meat sale rules vary by state; verify with the state agriculture department.
meat_rabbits.climate: Heat: buck fertility drops after several days above 85°F. Housing should be at least 10°F cooler than outside (Texas A&M).

sources.title: Bulletin #1044 Backyard Production of Meat Rabbits in Maine
Backyard Production of Meat Rabbits in Texas (Texas A&M AgriLife)

dairy_goats.minGroupSizeNote: MSU Extension calls goats herd animals but gives no minimum number.
dairy_goats.spaceIndoorNote: MSU Extension: 9 sq ft of open barn area per animal. Penn State meat-goat shelter: 10-12 sq ft per doe.
dairy_goats.pastureNote: MSU: an acre can support up to 6 goats under optimal conditions. The number varies strongly with rainfall, forage quality and browse.
dairy_goats.feedNote: Penn State: grain at 1 lb per 2.5-3 lb of milk. Forage is most of the diet. No annual hay tonnage was sourced.
dairy_goats.waterNote: MSU: 0.3-0.5 gal a day, up to 3 gal a day when lactating.

production.note: Penn State: varies by breed. Peak comes 4-6 weeks after kidding.

dairy_goats.laborNote: Penn State 50-doe commercial budget: about 15 h per doe per year (750 h total). Per-doe hours at household scale will be much higher because daily milking takes the same time for 1 or 50 does.
dairy_goats.startupNote: Penn State commercial (50 does): does $150-200 each, buildings and fencing $15,000-20,000, milking equipment $20,000-30,000. Not representative of a 2-doe household.
regulatory: Raw milk sale is state law and varies: May 2025 chart lists retail sales legal in about 13 states, on-farm only in about 16, herdshare only in a few, and prohibited or unaddressed in others. Verify with the state.

Penn State (2022) states raw milk sale is prohibited in Pennsylvania. The 2025 chart lists PA as a retail-legal (licensed) state. These sources conflict; treat as 'licensed permit required' and verify.
Grade A dairy rules: cool milk below 40°F immediately after milking (Penn State).
dairy_goats.predators: MSU: coyotes are the common predator. Guardian dog breeds such as Great Pyrenees, Anatolian and Kangal.
dairy_goats.welfare: MSU: quarantine new animals at least 40 days. Goats can live 10+ years.

sources.title: Dairy Goat Production (Penn State Agricultural Alternatives)
What to know before bringing home goats (Mississippi State Extension)
Updated Raw Milk Sales by State Chart (as of May 1, 2025), Food Safety News

meat_goats.starterFlockNote: NCAT and Penn State small commercial unit: 25 does and 1 buck. One buck can serve 25-50 does. No household-scale source was found.
meat_goats.pastureNote: Penn State: about 6-7 does per acre (0.14-0.17 acre each) on good pasture. NCAT: 0.5-1 goat per acre for brush maintenance (1-2 acres each). Depends on rainfall and forage.
meat_goats.feedNote: NCAT example: winter supplement 5 lb of dry matter a day for 120 days. Add 20% for hay waste.
meat_goats.waterNote: MSU Extension figure for goats in general.

production.kidsNote: Penn State under good management. NCAT budgets use a 144-180% kid crop with 10% death loss.

meat_goats.laborNote: NCAT citing an Oklahoma State budget: about 2 h per head per year plus 0.9-2 h of machinery labor.
meat_goats.startupNote: Penn State, 25 does + 1 buck, including fencing and equipment.
meat_goats.annualNote: NCAT: total cost per doe per year (operating $40-78 plus fixed $19-33). 2006-2009 data.
regulatory: Penn State cites state manure and nutrient-management rules (PA Clean Streams Law, Act 38).
meat_goats.predators: NCAT: guardian dogs. Fencing: 5-6 strand high-tensile electric or 47-in woven wire with 10-12 in vertical spacing, at least 4,000 V.

sources.title: Meat Goat Production (Penn State Agricultural Alternatives)
Meat Goats: Sustainable Production (ATTRA/NCAT)
What to know before bringing home goats (MSU Extension)

sheep.spaceIndoorNote: UMaine: about 15 sq ft per ewe. Cornell: a 900 sq ft barn holds up to 60 ewes with lambs.
sheep.pastureNote: Cornell Small Farms: start with no more than 2 ewes per acre. Stocking depends on pasture improvement, climate, soil and rotation.
sheep.feedNote: UMaine: about 3/4 ton of hay equivalent per ewe per year (1,500 lb), about half from grazing.
sheep.waterNote: NDSU (2026): pregnant ewes 1-2 gal, lactating ewes 2-3 gal, feeder lambs 1-1.5 gal a day. Intake rises with temperature.

production.lambsNote: UMaine: from under 1 to over 3 lambs per ewe a year.

sheep.welfare: UMaine: copper is toxic to sheep at lower levels than to other livestock, so do not use goat or cattle minerals.

sources.title: Bulletin #2186 Are You Thinking of Raising Sheep? (UMaine)
How to Get Started with Sheep (Cornell Small Farms)
Livestock Water Requirements AS1763 (NDSU)

feeder_pigs.unit: per pig, one grow-out (feeder about 50 lb to market)
feeder_pigs.pastureNote: Oregon State: 15-34 growing-finishing pigs per acre. Depends on soil, rainfall and rotation.
feeder_pigs.feedNote: Derived: Oregon State feed conversion of 2.5-3 lb feed per lb gain x (250-280 lb finish minus 50 lb start). Not stated directly by the source.
feeder_pigs.growOutNote: Derived from Oregon State's 1.5-2 lb/day gain over 200-230 lb of gain. Penn State describes about a May-to-November season. Oregon State: harvest at about 6 months of age.

production.note: UW-Madison example: 250 lb live at 70% dressing = 175 lb hot carcass, 169 lb chilled, about 125 lb retail cuts (67% cutting yield). Dressing is 70-75%. Bone-in cutting yield 74%, boneless 65%.

regulatory: Selling pork by the cut needs USDA- or state-inspected slaughter. Custom-exempt processing is for the owner's own use. No source was fetched for this; verify with the state.
feeder_pigs.climate: Oregon State: a 50-lb pig is comfortable at 70-82°F and pigs over 215 lb at 50-75°F. Penn State: pigs over 150 lb need cooling above about 70°F. Provide shade and a wallow.
feeder_pigs.welfare: Penn State: electric wire at ground level stops rooting under fences. Constant fresh water.

sources.title: Raising Small Groups of Pigs (Penn State)
Care and Management of New Feeder Pigs EM 9271 (Oregon State)
How much meat should a hog yield? (UW-Madison Extension)
Livestock Water Requirements AS1763 (NDSU)

production.honeyNote: USDA NASS: 48.0 lb per colony in 2025 and 51.7 lb in 2024 (operations with 5+ colonies). Penn State budget assumes 60 lb. First-year colonies often produce little surplus, though that was not sourced numerically.

honeybees.startupNote: Penn State (2012): $7,097.50 for 10 hives, including $2,000 facility adaptation. Equipment only is about $510 per hive.
honeybees.annualNote: Penn State (2012): $1,791.55 per year for 10 colonies.
regulatory: Apiary registration is required in some states, for example Pennsylvania (Penn State), Maryland, Illinois and Washington (state agency pages). Rules vary; check the state agriculture department.

sources.title: Agricultural Alternatives: Beekeeping (Penn State)
Honey (USDA NASS, March 2026)
Apiary Application for Registration of Honey Bee Colonies (Maryland)
Registration of Honeybee Colonies (Illinois)
Apiary Registration (Washington State Dept. of Agriculture)

turkeys.unit: per bird (Broad Breasted White), per grow-out
turkeys.spaceIndoorNote: Penn State: brooding 1-1.5 sq ft, growing 2-3, finishing 3-4. extension.org backyard: 6 sq ft.
turkeys.pastureNote: Penn State range stocking: 250 birds per acre.
turkeys.feedNote: MSU Extension (1978): about 105 lb per bird to 24 weeks. Modern strains reach market sooner (Penn State 14-17 wk), so actual feed may be lower. Old figure.
turkeys.growOutNote: Penn State: hens 14 wk (about 20 lb live), toms 17 wk (about 36 lb live).

production.dressedNote: MSU 1978: tom 25-30 lb live gives 19-24 lb dressed; hen 16-20 lb live gives about 14.5 lb dressed. Old data.

regulatory: The same USDA PPIA poultry exemptions (1,000 / 20,000 bird limits) apply to turkeys.
turkeys.welfare: Penn State: MG and blackhead can be serious for turkeys raised with chickens or on ground chickens used within 3-5 years.

sources.title: Small-Flock Turkey Production (Penn State)
E1259 Want to Raise a Few Turkeys? (Michigan State)
Space allowances for small and backyard poultry (extension.org)

eggs_small_flock.startupNote: Housing $1,500, feeders and waterers $250, brooding and misc $200. Excludes land and stock.
eggs_small_flock.laborNote: UMD: 0.5 h a day. Penn State egg business: 180-200 h a year.
eggs_small_flock.revenueNote: UMD: $16,842 over 2 years (3,208 dozen at $5 plus 80 stewing hens at $10), halved.
eggs_small_flock.netNote: UMD: $10,197 income over cash expenses in 2 years, halved. Excludes labor. $27.94 per labor hour. Cost per dozen $2.07.
eggs_small_flock.seasonality: Lay drops in short days and during molt without supplemental light (UF, UMN).
regulatory: Keep eggs at 45°F or below within 24 h of lay (Penn State). State egg-handler licensing and grading and labeling rules vary. Sales tax varies.

sources.title: Small Flock Layer Budget - 100 (UMD)
Small-Scale Egg Production (Penn State)

market_garden_per_acre.scale: Direct-market vegetable farms with under 3 acres in production (PASA benchmark study of 39 farms, tax years 2017-2019)
market_garden_per_acre.startupNote: No benchmark startup figure was found. One component: Penn State drip plus plastic mulch for 1 acre is about $9,850 (2016).
market_garden_per_acre.laborNote: PASA: half of farmers worked over 45 h/wk and a quarter over 55 h/wk (whole farm, in season).
market_garden_per_acre.revenueNote: PASA, farms under 3 acres: 25th-75th percentile. Median $46,413, 10th-90th percentile $19,882-64,820.
market_garden_per_acre.netNote: PASA, farms under 3 acres: 25th-75th percentile net margin, median 3%. Net income median $1,844 (IQR $77-6,435). Most direct-market vegetable farmers do not earn a middle-class income.
market_garden_per_acre.seasonality: Main season. Season extension with a high tunnel.
regulatory: FSMA Produce Safety Rule exemptions depend on sales volume (not sourced here). Sales tax. Liability insurance for markets.

sources.title: Financial Benchmarks for Direct-Market Vegetable Farms 2021 Report (PASA / SARE)
Drip Irrigation for Vegetable Production (Penn State)

market_garden_quarter_acre.scale: 0.25 acre, scaled linearly from the PASA per-acre figures for farms under 3 acres
market_garden_quarter_acre.revenueNote: PASA 25th-75th percentile per acre x 0.25. Linear scaling is an assumption. No quarter-acre study was found.
regulatory: As market_garden_per_acre.
risks: The linear scale-down may overstate or understate results

sources.title: Financial Benchmarks for Direct-Market Vegetable Farms 2021 Report (PASA / SARE)

microgreens.scale: 10x20 trays on a shelf system, 8 sq ft of infrastructure (MU budget)
microgreens.revenueNote: MU assumes $4.00/oz. Cycle 8-13.5 days, 27-46 cycles a year per position.
microgreens.netNote: MU: income over total costs per tray. Operating cost per tray $23.93-39.26. Packaging, labels and marketing ($16.30-24.30) are the largest costs.
regulatory: The MU budget has no regulatory notes. Microgreens are produce; state and local sale and food safety rules apply. Verify.

sources.title: Microgreens Planning Budget G693 (MU Extension)

cut_flowers.scale: Field-grown specialty cut flowers, 0.5-2 acres (the preferred emerging scale per Virginia Tech)
cut_flowers.laborNote: Virginia Tech: extremely labor- and time-intensive. Harvest is the biggest labor load.
cut_flowers.revenueNote: Virginia Tech citing a Growing for Market editor's estimate. Secondary estimate, not a budget.
cut_flowers.netNote: University of Tennessee cut-flower budgets (quarter-acre representative farm, 1,000 sq ft per crop) are at arec.tennessee.edu/budgets. Figures not extracted.
cut_flowers.seasonality: Spring to fall. Spring and fall shoulder seasons bring higher prices.
regulatory: Sales tax. Wholesale buyers pay 30-45 days out.
risks: local market saturation above about 10 acres

sources.title: Getting Started in the Production of Field-Grown Specialty Cut Flowers 426-618 (Virginia Tech)
TN Cut Flower Project Overview 2026 (UT/UK handout)

nursery_plants.landNote: UT: container production is typically 5-10 acres. Balled-and-burlapped field production must be over 10 acres to cash-flow. No small-scale bedding-plant source was found.
nursery_plants.startupNote: UT: pot-in-pot about $20,000 per acre from bare ground, or $15-25 per 10-gal pot position.
nursery_plants.seasonality: Spring peak for retail. Shade trees are about 5-year crops.
keySkills: irrigation (about 27,000 gal per acre per day for containers)
regulatory: State nursery certification and inspection is required. Example: Tennessee $200/yr, with the plant certificate traveling with each wholesale shipment.

sources.title: Getting Started in the Nursery Business (Univ. of Tennessee)

honey.revenueNote: Penn State (2012): includes pollination income. 600 lb honey at $5/lb retail. Wholesale was $1.50-2.00/lb then. NASS 2025: all-channel $3.05/lb, retail $7.15/lb.
regulatory: State apiary registration in some states. Honey labeling. Many states have cottage-food or honey-specific exemptions (not sourced here).

sources.title: Agricultural Alternatives: Beekeeping (Penn State)
Honey (USDA NASS, March 2026)

mushrooms_shiitake_logs.scale: About 100 logs to test and 500-1,000 logs commercially (Cornell, Virginia Tech)
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.landNote: Shaded woodlot or laying yard. No area figure was sourced.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.startupNote: Cornell 2019: about $12.06 per log including labor (spawn $0.75, wax $0.31). Virginia Tech budget: $1,626 for 500 logs.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.laborNote: Cornell 2019: about 60 min per log per year. Virginia Tech: 40 h to drill and inoculate 500 logs.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.yieldNote: Cornell: 1/4-1/2 lb per soaking and about 4 lb total. Virginia Tech 500-log budget: 1,690 lb over 4 years (about 3.4 lb per log), peaking in years 2-3. First fruiting 6-18 months after inoculation.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.priceNote: Cornell 2019: growers get $12-18, wholesale $10-12. Virginia Tech (2012 data): retail $10-20, wholesale $4-8.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.revenueNote: Derived: Virginia Tech 500-log budget peak year of 800 lb x $12.50.
mushrooms_shiitake_logs.seasonality: Cornell: about June to October in the Northeast (20-50 lb/wk from 500-1,000 logs).
regulatory: State rules for selling cultivated mushrooms vary. Not sourced.

sources.title: Economic Report for Log-Grown Shiitake Mushrooms (Cornell Small Farms)
The Basics of Hardwood-Log Shiitake Mushroom Production and Marketing ANR-102 (Virginia Tech)

mushrooms_oyster_indoor.scale: Indoor grow room, sawdust or straw blocks
mushrooms_oyster_indoor.yieldNote: University of Illinois trials (2015-2016): fresh yield per lb of substrate varied widely by strain and season. Cornell: halve the sawdust-block yield estimates for straw.
mushrooms_oyster_indoor.netNote: Cornell Small Farms indoor production page.
mushrooms_oyster_indoor.priceNote: The only extension price found was $1.91-3.74/lb for 2000-2016 wholesale (Illinois). Too old for direct-market use.
mushrooms_oyster_indoor.seasonality: Year-round with climate control (65-75°F; incubation 4-8 weeks at 65-70°F).
regulatory: Not sourced. Verify state food-safety rules for fresh mushrooms.

sources.title: Indoor Production (Cornell Small Farms Program)
Small-scale Production of Oyster Mushroom (D.K. Lee, J. Shafer)

value_added_cottage_food.scale: Home-kitchen cottage food business (jams, baked goods)
value_added_cottage_food.startupNote: IJ 2017 survey median startup capital (775 producers in 22 states).
regulatory: Cottage food law varies by state (IJ 2022): 25 states cap annual sales ($3,000 to $250,000), 19 limit the allowed food list, 8 ban online sales, 15 ban mail delivery, and 6 plus DC require extensive licensing and inspection.
Low-acid or non-approved foods usually need a licensed kitchen or processor license. Sales tax. Product liability insurance is advisable.

sources.title: Flour Power: cottage foods survey (Institute for Justice)
New Report Grades Each State's Laws for Homemade Food Sales (Institute for Justice, Baking Bad)

agritourism.scale: U-pick, farm stays, events; any farm reporting agritourism income
agritourism.revenueNote: 2022 Census of Agriculture national average agritourism income per farm reporting it (via UGA factsheet). Georgia average $41,849. The average is skewed by large operations. US total $1.26B in 2022, up 12.4% real from 2017 (ERS).
agritourism.seasonality: Fall peak for pumpkins and corn mazes. U-pick follows crop season.
regulatory: Many states have agritourism limited-liability statutes. Protection usually requires posted warning signs (for example Minnesota 604A.40).
Insurance: farm property, general liability, product liability, event liability, livestock coverage. UMN notes coverage is not cheap. Get written confirmation of which activities are covered.
Zoning and health permits for lodging and food service vary locally.

sources.title: 2022 Census of Agriculture: majority of U.S. counties generate some agritourism income (USDA ERS)
Agritourism and Direct Marketing census factsheet AGECON24-01-14 (UGA)
Insurance and liability considerations for agritourism (UMN Extension)

meat_birds_pastured_broilers.scale: 100 birds per batch, 7 batches a year = 700 birds (MU small-scale budget)
meat_birds_pastured_broilers.revenueNote: MU: 4.55 lb dressed at $4.00/lb. That price is below current direct-market prices; recompute with local prices.
meat_birds_pastured_broilers.netNote: MU budget shows a loss at both scales: -$7.61 per bird for 700/yr and -$0.63 per bird for 4,900/yr at $4/lb. Small scale does not pay at that price.
regulatory: USDA PPIA Producer/Grower 1,000-bird and 20,000-bird exemptions. No interstate sales. Label 'Exempt P.L. 90-492'. State rules may be stricter (ACES 2022). Penn State has guidance on marketing exempt poultry.

sources.title: Mobile Poultry for Meat Planning Budget G742 (MU Extension)
A Quick Guide to Raising Pastured Broilers (Penn State)
Exemptions from USDA Inspection for Small-Scale Poultry Processors (Alabama Extension)
Marketing poultry slaughtered under USDA exemption (Penn State)

raised_bed_4x8.note: No extension or reliable cost source was retrieved in this pass. Leave unsourced.

drip_irrigation.note: HomeGuide (2025): DIY installation $0.50-1.00/sq ft, professional $1.50-4.50/sq ft ($1,500-4,500 per 1,000 sq ft), farm field above-ground $500-3,000/acre. Penn State (2016): drip tape $1.50-2.50 per 100 ft; a full 1-acre system with pump, filters and mulch about $9,850.

sources.title: Drip irrigation system cost (HomeGuide; commercial cost guide)

deer_fence.note: Purdue FNR-486 (2014): 7.5-ft polypropylene mesh, about $1.50/ft materials, lasts 6-8 years, cuts browse 60-98%. Heavy-duty mesh costs about twice as much per foot. Old price.

sources.title: FNR-486-W deer exclusion fencing (Purdue Extension)

livestock_fence.note: MU Extension G1193, prices as of January 2024: 1,320-ft perimeter, gently rolling ground, one gate and one stream crossing, materials plus labor. Short runs and many corners cost more per foot.

sources.title: Fence construction cost G1193 (MU Extension)
Estimated Costs for Livestock Fencing B1-75 (Iowa State Ag Decision Maker)

high_tunnel.note: Purdue Veg Crops Hotline (2016): high tunnels $2-7/sq ft, heated greenhouses $7-30/sq ft. Arkansas FSA-6147: a 30x96 ft self-built tunnel cost $1.30/sq ft at fall-2009 prices (very old). NRCS EQIP practice 325 (High Tunnel System) offers cost-share. The tunnel must be kept for the 5-year practice life. A vendor guide (2026) cites typical EQIP payment rates of about $5-12/sq ft depending on state and producer status; confirm with the local NRCS office.

sources.title: Cost Considerations Prior to the Purchase of a High Tunnel or Greenhouse (Purdue)

preservation.safetyNote: NCHFP: use only up-to-date, research-tested recipes such as the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015 revision) and So Easy to Preserve. If a tested recipe was not followed, all jars, sealed or not, may be unsafe and should be discarded. Low-acid foods must be pressure canned; acid foods (fruits, acidified tomatoes, jams and jellies, pickles) may be processed in a boiling-water canner.

canning.note: NCHFP: for best quality, can no more than you will use within a year. Store at 50-70°F. Avoid above 95°F, hot pipes and direct sun.
suits: low-acid vegetables, meats, beans (pressure canner only)

freezing.note: NCHFP, at 0°F or below. These are quality limits; food stays safe longer. Blanch vegetables first and use moisture-vapor-resistant packaging.

dehydrating.note: NCHFP: dried fruits last about 1 year at 60°F and 6 months at 80°F. Vegetables last about half as long as fruits. Store cool, dry and dark, in glass so moisture is visible.

root_cellar.note: UAF (2020) at stated conditions. Groups: cold and very moist (32-40°F, 90-95% RH): beets, carrots, radishes, turnips, parsnips, kohlrabi, cabbage. Cold and moist: potatoes (38-40°F, 80-90%). Cool and dry: onions, garlic (32-35°F, 60-70%). Warm and dry: winter squash, pumpkins (50-55°F, 60-75%). Sweet potatoes: 50°F+, 80-90% (MU). Store apples apart from vegetables (MU).

curing.note: Iowa State (2025). Winter squash: cure at 80-85°F, 80-85% RH (not acorn types), store at 50-55°F (acorn lasts 5-8 weeks). Sweet potatoes: home cure 10-14 days warm and shaded, store at 55-60°F, 85-90% RH. Onions: cure 2-3 weeks warm, dry and ventilated, store at 32-40°F, 65-70% RH. Garlic: cure warm and dry, store the same way. Potatoes: cure at 50-60°F, 85-90% RH for 2 weeks, store at 40°F, 90-95% RH, in the dark.
